items.title: Ethanol debut for WinGD as Maersk vessel makes landmark US bunkering and voyage
items.original_title: Ethanol debut for WinGD as Maersk vessel makes landmark US bunkering and voyage
items.summary: WinGD has recorded the first in-service operation of its X-DF-M/E alcohol fuel engine platform on ethanol fuel, following a successful bunkering and voyage in the US. The 9,000 TEU container ship Tangier Maersk, owned by the Maersk shipping line, successfully sailed from Houston to New York on ethanol fuel. The vessel took on the bunker at the Port of Houston in late September, with the world’s largest bioethanol producer POET supplying fuel for the WinGD X82DF-Mengine powering the vessel. The occasion marked the first marine bunkering of a 100% bioethanol blend in the US, and the first ever in-service bunkering of ethanol to a WinGD engine. The first X-DF-M/E engine capable of using methanol entered service in 2025, with multi-alcohol fuel capability added this year – enabling both methanol and ethanol fuel to be used on six mid-sized sister vessels ordered by Maersk. (Image credit: Alabama Port Authority) WinGD Vice President Research & Development Sebastian Hensel said: “The use of bioethanol as a marine fuel is a natural progression for WinGD after successful operating experience with methanol using the same engine platform. This debut, a result of the strong momentum of Maersk in validating the use of this cost-effective low-carbon fuel, enabled us to confirm important operational and safety functions.

items.title: Canadian wheat outlook improves as harvest advances, quality fears ease
items.original_title: Canadian wheat outlook improves as harvest advances, quality fears ease
items.summary: The outlook for Canada’s spring wheat crop has become more optimistic as improving harvest conditions and better-than-feared quality results ease concerns over widespread crop deterioration, while strong grain movements through Vancouver provide further confidence in the export market. After weeks of heavy rainfall across the Canadian Prairies raised concerns over sprouting, lower falling numbers and potential downgrades, market participants said recent harvest progress suggested that overall wheat quality could be better than initially expected. “Sounds like harvest is making progress in Canada with drier weather and not as much feed wheat as previously concerned,” a trader said. “Very hard in some areas to find 13.5% pro,” the trader said, explaining that exporters holding larger volumes of lower-protein wheat could offer wider protein spreads to manage their inventories. Market participants said the spread had expanded considerably beyond typical levels, reflecting regional differences in crop quality and the difficulty of sourcing wheat that meets specific milling requirements. The improving crop outlook has therefore not translated into uniformly weaker basis levels, as limited farmer selling, regional protein shortages and varying export capacity continue to support physical wheat values. Still, the combination of better-than-feared crop quality, advancing harvest activity and strong grain transportation has contributed to a more constructive outlook than earlier in the season.

items.title: InterManager Warns Enclosed Space Deaths Demand Urgent Industry Action
items.original_title: InterManager Warns Enclosed Space Deaths Demand Urgent Industry Action
items.summary: InterManager has called for urgent industry action on enclosed space safety after its latest research highlighted persistent failures in procedures, training, leadership and accident prevention. The organisation has recorded 354 enclosed space accidents over the past 30 years, between 1996 and 2026, across tankers, bulkers, general cargo ships, passenger vessels, containerships and other vessel types. Its latest seafarer survey identifies a recurring gap between safety procedures and operational reality onboard. InterManager says this must now be enhanced to deliver competence, rather than just training, particularly as enclosed space entry training is being considered as part of the current review of STW requirements, with the International Chamber of Shipping leading industry input. InterManager will explore the survey findings and wider enclosed space safety concerns during a webinar, run in conjunction with The Nautical Institute, on 27 October 2026 at 10am GMT. The webinar will bring together industry experts, Captain Pradeep Chawla, CEO of Marie Pals, Captain Garry Hallett from InterManager and Richard Cowburn, human factors specialist, to discuss where the industry stands now on enclosed space safety, how seafarers and shore-based stakeholders feel about current practice, and what practical action is needed next.

items.title: Danica Urges Shipping Industry to Manage Crew Turnover, Not Just Retention
items.original_title: Danica Urges Shipping Industry to Manage Crew Turnover, Not Just Retention
items.summary: Shipping companies need to pay as much attention to managing crew turnover as they do to retaining seafarers if they are to maintain safe and efficient vessel operations, according to Henrik Jensen, founder and CEO of Danica Crewing Specialists. Speaking ahead of this week’s Crew Connect Global 2026 in Manila (20-22 October), Mr Jensen warned that while retaining experienced seafarers remains a priority, changing attitudes towards employment mean shipowners and managers must accept that some crew turnover is inevitable and be better prepared to manage it. “Having a stable crew pool makes a significant difference to the safe and efficient operation of a vessel. We also need to think about how we manage these changes when they happen.” Mr Jensen explained that traditional retention strategies, including competitive salaries, bonuses, insurance, pensions and promotion opportunities, have largely been built around the expectations of older generations, who tend to value stability and long-term employment. Mr Jensen believes shipping companies should focus on making it easier for new crew members to familiarise themselves with onboard equipment, procedures and working practices.

Far less attention goes to a quieter question: where are these carbon decisions actually made, and who can see the data behind them? In commodity trades, the choice between CIF and FOB helps decide who absorbs it. Carbon has moved beyond the charter party and into the commodity contract. items.original_title: Oil tanker on fire after hitting mine in Hormuz: Iran’s Guards
items.summary: Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said Monday an oil tanker caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz after hitting a mine, the latest such incident since Tehran tightened its grip of the waterway. Iran seized control of the strait after war broke out against the United States and Israel late February, choking off the vital shipping route which normally carries about a fifth of the world’s oil. The Islamic republic has demanded that all ships seek its authorisation before transiting. “An oil tanker, which was in violation, struck a naval mine south of the Strait of Hormuz, resulting in an explosion and a fire in its engine room,” Iranian state media quoted the Guards as saying. The tanker was travelling in the strait’s “unauthorized southern route” and had disabled its positioning and navigation systems, the statement said. It came a day after the Guards said two oil tankers caught fire in the strait, both after hitting mines. The Guards’ naval commander Admiral Ali Ozmaei warned this week that any vessel that deactivated its navigation systems would be considered “hostile.” The United States has imposed a naval counter-blockade on Iranian oil exports in response to Tehran’s blockade on the waterway. items.title: Tankers: Is a Clean Slate Coming for 15% of the Tanker Fleet?

items.summary: According to Gibson, “some 878 tankers, 15% of the trading fleet, are under sanctions, rising to 25% for Aframax/LR2s. The US can only waive its own designations, however, and EU and UK cooperation looks unlikely. That leaves 325 tankers listed by OFAC alone as the possible pool, and 153 of them are VLCCs, covering almost all of the 164 sanctioned VLCCs. Only 28 of the 116 sanctioned Suezmaxes and 42 of the 322 Aframax/LR2s are OFAC-only, and clean tonnage is limited, as around 40 CPP MRs, mostly in the East, potentially available for mainstream trade. The length of any waiver matters too, as a short-term reprieve may not be enough for charterers to commit to longer voyages, and the risk of renewed tensions after next month’s midterm elections may further limit appetite”, the shipbroker said. Most of the tonnage it could add is old, mostly VLCCs, sitting East of Suez. Since any delisting would follow OFAC’s usual full review, it may take time for a significant number of ships to be freed for mainstream trade. The TD3C VLCC FFA market has corrected downwards over the past couple of days, in part due to this news. In the end, the number of waivers given out will decide whether any impact is felt at all”, Gibson concluded.

In response to the Middle East situation and to ensure a stable supply of energy to Japan, METI said the government will establish a program under which it will partially compensate non-life insurance companies for the funds required to pay insurance claims under marine property insurance, such as cargo and hull insurance, covering the transportation of crude oil, oil products and LNG, even in cases where the provision of reinsurance is prohibited. “To address such circumstances, the government will establish a mechanism to fill the gap left by the unavailable foreign reinsurance coverage.” Japan introduced a law in 2012 to compensate P&I cover as a sovereign guarantee for each tanker carrying Iranian crude amid EU sanctions against Iran — an initiative that remains in effect to date. items.title: What lessons can we learn from declining carrier schedule adherence and rising port congestion?
items.original_title: What lessons can we learn from declining carrier schedule adherence and rising port congestion?
items.summary: Look at it from the viewpoint of a shipper moving goods by containership on the Asia-Europe route. The proportion of ships on this route which arrived on the scheduled day of arrival declined from 51% in May to just 31% in September (average of all ports and all carriers), according to the Drewry Container Capacity Insight. Even the Gemini alliance, which has a higher-than-average track record for on-time arrivals, managed just 34% in September. The Asia-Europe trade’s schedule reliability scores by carrier in September ranged between 19% and 38% and the proportion of sailings not cancelled ranged between 0% and 23%, according to Drewry’s analysis for this route. Looking at this from a carrier viewpoint, the logic is that cargo volumes were strong in the peak season, port congestion got worse in Asia, but the carriers could make higher profits by throwing more ship capacity at the market and cancelling fewer sailings… which must have made port congestion worse. At Drewry, we are looking more closely at how carrier performance, port congestion and network exposure can be brought together to give shippers a clearer picture of where they may be vulnerable. Ultimately, the aim should be to move away from simply reacting to delays and towards building those risks into carrier selection, procurement strategies and contingency planning.

items.original_title: AVS+ targets fragmented vessel procurement with centralised fleet management platform
items.summary: AVS Global Ship Supply has developed AVS +, a digital platform designed to give ship managers greater visibility and control over vessel procurement by bringing ordering, expenditure, inventory and operational records into a single system. The platform addresses a common challenge in maritime procurement, where orders, quotations, invoices and operational information can be spread across emails, telephone conversations and separate files, making it difficult for managers to establish the status of an order or obtain an up-to-date view of vessel expenditure. Through AVS+, customers can manage supply activities covering provisions, technical stores and port services through one web-based application. Fleet information is presented through both interactive map and list views, giving users access to vessel-specific operational records and invoices from a central repository. The system also allows companies to define procurement and catering parameters at fleet level, including target victualling rates, portion weights and supply lead times, while retaining the flexibility to adjust those requirements for individual vessels. The installation, completed at a shipyard outfitting site in Shanghai, makes the 168-meter vessel the largest RoRo ship equipped with wind-assisted propulsion and gives it more mechanical sails than any other ship, according to LD Armateurs and Finnish wind propulsion specialist Norsepower. Airbus expects the new fleet to cut annual emissions from its transatlantic shipping operations by more than half, from approximately 68,000 metric tons of CO2 in 2023 to 33,000 metric tons by 2030. “Completing installation of six Norsepower Rotor Sails on Spirit of Toulouse is a significant milestone for wind propulsion in the RoRo segment,” said Heikki Pöntynen, CEO of Norsepower. The project comes as wind-assisted propulsion moves beyond individual demonstration projects and finds wider use across the commercial shipping fleet. Earlier this year, Berge Bulk completed the installation of four folding rotor sails on its 208,000-dwt Newcastlemax bulk carrier Berge Meru , following a similar project aboard the larger Berge Neblina in 2024.

The true extent of attacks on merchant ships in the Strait of Hormuz remains unclear, with a new report from UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) acknowledging that most vessels struck in the region are not reporting incidents directly to the maritime security organization. In its weekly overview published Friday , UKMTO said it is struggling to establish the true number of attacks because the majority of vessels targeted are refusing to submit reports. UKMTO recorded 12 attacks during its latest reporting period, including 10 in the Strait of Hormuz, one in the Arabian Gulf and one in the Gulf of Oman. UKMTO’s latest report adds that most vessels broadcasting AIS continue to use the Iranian route, even as U.S.-facilitated traffic accounts for the majority of reported transits. And with UKMTO now acknowledging that most attacked vessels are not reporting incidents directly, even the growing number of documented strikes may offer only a partial picture of the dangers facing seafarers.

Together with the EU’s full ban on imports of Russian LNG from January 2027, this shortfall could require the bloc to cut winter gas demand by 7%, or 14bcm, compared with last winter. Gas demand creeps up as imports stay flat Before 2022, EU gas storage was a seasonal buffer: fill in summer, withdraw in winter, with flexible (mainly Russian) pipeline imports absorbing demand swings. Storage’s share of EU winter gas consumption rose from 25% in 2021–22 to 30% in 2025–26, with a five-year high of 33% in 2024–25, according to Eurostat. Winter gas consumption fell sharply from roughly 222bcm in 2021–22 to around 185bcm in 2022–23, as high prices and emergency gas-saving measures cut demand. items.title: LNG, methanol and B24 bunkered at Ningbo-Zhoushan on same day
items.original_title: LNG, methanol and B24 bunkered at Ningbo-Zhoushan on same day
items.summary: This was the first time three different marine fuels had been supplied on the same day to different vessels berthed at the same port in China, according to the Ningbo Maritime Safety Administration (MSA). The LNG bunker vessel Haiyang Shiyou 302 delivered around 7,400 cbm (3,300 mt) of LNG at the Chuanshan port area on 30 September. The methanol bunker vessel Zhongran Green Energy 85 supplied around 7,500 mt of methanol at Meishan terminal, while Sijie 21 delivered around 3,000 mt of B24 biofuel blend at Daxie terminal. The three bunkering operations marked the first time in China that three different marine fuels were supplied simultaneously to vessels berthed at the same port, according to the Ningbo MSA. “The ‘one port, three supplies’ model signifies a diversified and large-scale breakthrough” in the alternative fuel bunkering capacity of Ningbo-Zhoushan Port, Ningbo MSA added. On 28 September, Sinobunker’s bunker vessel Daqing 268 supplied 300 mt of bio-methanol to COSCO’s container ship Carnation at the Nansha terminal in the Port of Guangzhou. The operation followed an earlier delivery by Daqing 268 of around 1,000 mt of pure bio-methanol to NYK Group’s dual-fuel bulk carrier Green Future at Guangzhou’s Lantau Anchorage. These two deliveries demonstrate Guangzhou Port’s ability to handle methanol bunkering at both terminals and anchorages, according to the port authority.

items.title: Dry bulk safety: scrap metal fires, fumigation and enclosed spaces
items.original_title: Dry bulk safety: scrap metal fires, fumigation and enclosed spaces
items.summary: BIMCO’s Dry Bulk Cargo Network discussed three persistent safety challenges at its latest meeting: fire risks from contaminated scrap metal cargoes, the shift of fumigation duties from specialists to ships’ crews, and continuing fatalities in enclosed spaces. Members highlighted the need for clearer cargo information, stronger charter party provisions, and practical measures to protect crews. The eighth meeting of the BIMCO Dry Bulk Cargo Network was held on Thursday 8 October 2026 and covered the following agenda items: Scrap metals had previously been discussed at the sixth meeting in early 2025, when views differed over whether the IMSBC Code schedule for scrap adequately covers the different types of scrap and the effects of contamination by materials such as plastics, tyres, and oils. These include questions about the meaning of “as dry as possible;” surveyors finding more plastics, tyres, oils and flammable material than the declared impurity percentage suggests; and the implications of lithium batteries being present, including whether this introduces dangerous goods considerations under Class 9 of the IMDG Code. These include confusion about the distinction between different scrap metal cargoes and how they should be described and classified, and a general lack of understanding of the hazards.

items.title: Asian refiners face margin squeeze from record tanker costs
items.original_title: Asian refiners face margin squeeze from record tanker costs
items.summary: The cost of shipping oil in supertankers has reached record highs, putting pressure on profit margins for Asian oil refiners who rely heavily on Middle Eastern crude, the International Energy Agency said in a monthly report. Asian refiners have encountered the highest transportation costs as cargoes move through the Strait of Hormuz to secondary tankers for onward delivery, the IEA said. The freight rate for a Very Large Crude Carrier on a route from the Middle East Gulf to Asia had climbed to around $36 per barrel by early October, more than five times the cost before the Iran war, the agency added. Refiners can partially offset this by purchasing US crude, but those freight rates have also increased, with costs for the US Gulf Coast to China route exceeding $37 per barrel, the IEA said. The rise in delivered crude costs pushed margins for Asian refiners processing medium sour crude into negative territory in September, the agency said. Source: Investing.com

items.title: Reinforcing the ETS SMAP to guarantee long-term shipping decarbonisation
items.original_title: Reinforcing the ETS SMAP to guarantee long-term shipping decarbonisation
items.summary: The SMAP mechanism introduced under the ETS represents an opportunity to help the maritime sector to transition towards clean fuels and propulsion technologies, and strengthen Europe’s industrial leadership. With an estimated support of €15 billion between 2028 and 2040, such a mechanism could encourage shipping companies to use green e-fuels, which will need to be scaled up in this period to meet long-term decarbonisation targets. The European Commission’s Sustainable Transport Investment Plan (STIP) mentions that in less than a decade, 4.6 million tonnes of e-fuels could be needed to reach FuelEU targets. A high price difference coverage in favour of e-fuels compared to other alternative fuels under SMAP is a welcome step, but is unlikely to be sufficient in itself to ensure a genuine move towards e-fuels. Because of the capital-intensive nature of e-fuels production, these projects will require producers to enter long-term offtake agreements with companies in order to secure investment. The current SMAP proposal is unlikely to provide sufficient support to this process. While some alternative fuels and zero-emissions propulsion technologies have a role to play in reducing maritime GHG emissions, SMAP should be used primarily to reward long-term e-fuel use, rather than short-term fuel and propulsion technological options which may already be incentivised under existing legislation.

items.summary: Indonesian coal miners and Asian buyers are holding back on signing 2027 term supply contracts as uncertainty over government-approved production quotas and changes to export rules clouds the supply outlook, with some miners adding protective clauses to any deals, market sources told Platts. The delays come as Indonesia prepares to transition to a new export framework from Jan. 1, 2027, giving a bigger role to PT Danantara Sumberdaya Indonesia, or DSI, in supervising strategic commodity exports, including coal. “We might sign an umbrella contract for 2027 with a pre-condition of subject to RKAB approval. “Not hearing any 2027 contract till now, but if any, contracts now will be subject to various conditions,” another miner told Platts. The uncertainty comes as miners are also waiting to know how much coal they will be allowed to produce in 2027. If the production approved remains at 2026 levels, the market could remain tight in 2027 as well,” a large Asian buyer of Indonesian coal said. Price implications The tighter supply situation has already pushed Indonesian coal prices higher in 2026. Market participants said progress on 2027 contracts would depend in part on greater clarity over miners’ approved production volumes, DMO commitments and how the new export system will operate from January.

items.title: Korea’s Integrated Ship Survivability Design Framework
items.original_title: Korea’s Integrated Ship Survivability Design Framework
items.summary: A Korean-developed integrated design framework has been developed to comprehensively analyze “ship survivability”—a naval vessel’s ability to avoid enemy attack, withstand damage when hit, restore key functions after damage, and continue its mission. The key achievement is the integration of survivability analyses that had previously been performed using separate software tools into a single software environment. The AX Convergence Research Center of the Virtual Engineering Platform Research Division at the Korea Institute of Machinery and Materials (KIMM, President Seog-Hyeon Ryu) developed ‘isSAFE,’ an integrated ship survivability design framework. isSAFE provides an integrated design environment in which a ship model can be built, various weapon hit scenarios can be generated, and vulnerability, recoverability, and results analyses can be performed in a continuous workflow. Ship survivability consists of three elements: susceptibility, the ability to avoid enemy detection and attack; vulnerability, the ability to withstand damage when hit; and recoverability, the ability to restore key functions after damage. This enables users to compare survivability under different ship configurations and conditions and is expected to support the Republic of Korea Navy (ROK Navy), shipyards, and other end users in ship design and survivability assessments.

items.title: China: Coal use reaching peak plateau amid green goals
items.original_title: China: Coal use reaching peak plateau amid green goals
items.summary: China’s coal consumption is expected to enter a peak plateau transition during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-30), following a steady deceleration in growth as the country’s green energy transformation reshapes its economic fundamentals, said a think tank. During the 14th Five-Year Plan period (2021-25), the country’s coal usage was characterized by rising total volume but a markedly slowing growth rate, according to the Report on China Energy Development 2026, released by the China Electric Power Planning and Engineering Institute in Beijing. In 2025, total coal consumption reached 4.76 billion metric tons, edging up a mere 0.1 percent year-on-year. During the 15th Five-Year Plan period, as China accelerates the construction of a new energy system, promotes the clean and efficient utilization of coal, upgrades traditional industries and replaces scattered coal — referring to coal of poor quality which is used throughout the civil sector for household cooking, heating and various commercial applications — national coal consumption will enter a peak plateau period, the report said. The steel and building materials sectors — which account for about 15 percent and 6 percent of coal consumption, respectively — also registered declines.

items.title: UK ports hit back at Brussels over ETS diversion claims
items.original_title: UK ports hit back at Brussels over ETS diversion claims
items.summary: British ports have challenged European Union claims that shipping lines are diverting container traffic to the UK to escape carbon charges, warning that proposed anti-evasion measures risk penalising billions of pounds of investment in British terminals. The British Ports Association (BPA) has rejected findings from Spain’s EU ETS Observatory linking rising UK container activity to the bloc’s Emissions Trading System, arguing that new capacity, changing liner networks and commercial competition offer more convincing explanations. In a new report, the association said around 85% of the UK’s container traffic growth in 2025 was concentrated in London, following the opening of DP World’s £350m ($465m) fourth berth at London Gateway in late 2024. Government figures show UK ports handled 11% more containers last year, equivalent to an additional 600,000 units. The association also disputes treating the widely cited 76% figure as evidence of carbon-driven diversion specifically to Britain, arguing that the available analysis does not isolate the effects of ETS from alliance restructuring, congestion and new terminal capacity. The disagreement comes after the European Commission proposed tightening rules designed to prevent containerships from using neighbouring non-EU ports to reduce their ETS exposure.

items.title: Liquimar lines up suezmax trio at New Hantong
items.original_title: Liquimar lines up suezmax trio at New Hantong
items.summary: Greek tanker owner Liquimar Tankers has been linked to an order for three suezmax newbuildings in China, adding fresh crude carrier capacity after cashing in on the strong secondhand tanker market. The Dimitris Papadimitriou-controlled company has contracted three 157,000 dwt vessels at Jiangsu New Hantong Ship Heavy Industry, according to shipbuilding sources. The conventionally fuelled tankers are scheduled for delivery in the second half of 2030, with pricing estimated at just under $86m apiece, putting the potential investment at close to $258m. The pair changed hands for a reported $68m each, generating approximately $136m in gross sale proceeds. Liquimar has already emerged behind another Chinese tanker project this year. In August, shipbuilding intelligence identified the company as the owner of the 113,500 dwt aframax/LR2 Priamos under construction at Hengli Heavy Industries. Liquimar was set up in 1990, as a way for its parent company, Dioryx Maritime Corp, to expand from dry cargo and containerships into the oil tanker sector, before becoming a standalone entity in 1995. The latest reported deal would add another name to New Hantong’s suezmax orderbook. Earlier this year, Eyal Ofer’s Zodiac Maritime contracted four suezmaxes at the Chinese yard for 2029 delivery, taking its programme in the segment to nine vessels.

items.summary: South Korea’s HMM is pressing ahead with its fleet expansion programme, approving a $1.62bn investment in 12 containerships comprising eight 13,000 teu newbuildings and four smaller vessels. The Seoul-listed carrier’s board approved spending KRW2.168trn ($1.617bn) yesterday, according to a stock exchange filing. The investment includes fresh orders for eight 13,000 teu ships, alongside the acquisition of three 2,800 teu vessels and one 1,700 teu ship through resale transactions involving newbuildings already under construction. The 12 vessels will add a combined 114,100 teu of capacity, with deliveries scheduled to be completed by December 2029. HMM has yet to identify the shipyards responsible for the eight larger vessels or the sellers of the four smaller ships. Propulsion specifications have also not been disclosed. The latest investment follows last year’s KRW4trn ($2.8bn) commitment covering 12 LNG dual-fuel 13,000 teu containerships and two VLCCs, with HD Hyundai and Hanwha Ocean securing the boxship contracts. Under HMM’s business plan through to 2030, the carrier aims to expand its containership fleet to 166 vessels totalling 1.47m teu by the end of the decade, alongside 110 bulk carriers with a combined capacity of 13.52m dwt.

items.title: West Africa’s ore boom meets China’s growing VLOC armada
items.original_title: West Africa’s ore boom meets China’s growing VLOC armada
items.summary: West Africa is fast becoming dry bulk shipping’s biggest growth engine, with its mineral export boom poised to absorb the equivalent of another 120 capesizes by 2030. UK consultancy Tradeviews forecasts in a new report that shipments from the region will surge 50% from 2025 levels to 303m tonnes by the end of the decade, with Guinea’s giant Simandou iron ore project leading the charge. Crucially for shipowners, the long voyages to China will magnify the impact on vessel demand. Liberian iron ore exports nearly doubled to 10.1m tonnes. Tradeviews expects regional exports to reach 267m tonnes next year, with Guinean iron ore shipments climbing to 45m tonnes in 2027 and approximately 112m tonnes by 2030. Tradeviews calculates that moving a tonne from West Africa consequently absorbs around 2.6 times as much vessel time. On this basis, the consultancy estimates West African trades will require the equivalent of 330 capesizes by 2030, compared with 210 last year. The broker described the situation as a “test of elasticity” rather than the start of another cargo boom, pointing out that Shandong alumina refineries processing imported ore lost RMB261.8 per tonne in September.

The CSSC-controlled yard has signed a framework agreement with China Railway Shanhaiguan Bridge Group, bringing the heavy-steel fabricator into its shipbuilding operations. GSI said its expanding orderbook and increasingly complex vessel mix would drive up demand for hull blocks over the coming years, prompting the move to bring in additional manufacturing capacity. The China Railway Construction Corporation subsidiary is fabricating 10 cargo-hold bottom sections weighing up to 96 tonnes each, which are to be transported to Shanghai for final assembly. The company has established three outdoor block assembly lines and is targeting annual ship block production of up to 100,000 tonnes, with longer-term ambitions to move into complete vessel construction. items.title: Ship Fuel Market Fragments as Middle East Conflict Hits Trade
items.original_title: Ship Fuel Market Fragments as Middle East Conflict Hits Trade
items.summary: A general view shows the Novorossiysk Fuel Oil Terminal (NMT) in the Black Sea port of Novorossiisk, Russia May 30, 2018. Picture taken May 30, 2018. REUTERS/Natalya Chumakova Oct 15, 2026 (Bloomberg) –Shipowners are facing an increasingly fragmented fuel market as disruptions triggered by the Middle East conflict raise concerns about the availability and quality of supply. “No one can treat bunkering as a routine, last-minute decision anymore,” said Frederik Guttormsen, Asia Pacific president at Stolt-Nielsen Ltd., an operator of 167 tankers that transport chemicals worldwide. “We’re securing fuel earlier and tracking availability and lead times at key ports because the risk is now as much about prompt supply as about price.” Middle East oil flows are coming under renewed strain from recent attacks in the region, including on vessels transiting Hormuz. Disruptions are also becoming more frequent, leading to vessel diversions that are shifting fuel demand to other locations, said Peter Grünwaldt , head of bunkering at tanker owner Hafnia Ltd. “We’re making sure we have fuel available at these ports,” he said. Saudi Arabia is looking at ways to expand its oil pipeline capacity to destinations outside the Persian Gulf to 10 million barrels a day within two to three years, said Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman.

items.title: UK port volume growth not due to EU shippers avoiding ETS, says BPA
items.original_title: UK port volume growth not due to EU shippers avoiding ETS, says BPA
items.summary: UK lobbyists today pushed back at attempts to have the EU designate the ports of Felixstowe, London, and Southampton as “neighbouring container transhipment ports”, in the ongoing question of whether shippers are rerouting cargo to avoid ETS scheme charges. In July, the EU ETS Observatory – developed by Spain’s state-owned ports administrator Puertos del Estado as a way of monitoring “carbon leakage” from its transhipment hub of Algeciras to Morocco’s Tanger Med after the introduction of EU-ETS at the beginning of 2024 – published a report which appeared to suggest that the container volume growth seen in UK ports during 2025 was the direct result of shippers seeking to minimise EU-ETS charges. It had led to a “reduction in the connectivity of container traffic for long-distance services operated at EU ports, compared with neighbouring countries not subject to European environmental regulations, measured in terms of the teu-mile parameter”. However, the British Ports Association (BPA) today argued that 2025’s volume growth seen at the UK’s three main ports was caused by a combination of new capacity coming onstream at London Gateway and the reorganisation of the deepsea shipping alliances that took place at the start of the year.

items.title: Low Rhine water level driving barge cargo to capacity-strained road and rail
items.original_title: Low Rhine water level driving barge cargo to capacity-strained road and rail
items.summary: Terminals at Antwerp and Rotterdam are coming under growing pressure as unseasonably low water along the Rhine continues to restrict container barge movements on the river, with cargo being pushed towards already-constrained rail and road networks. SeasC4U’s Gunther Ginckels told The Loadstar barges around Duisburg-Ruhrort were operating at roughly two-thirds of normal capacity, while vessels further upstream were carrying substantially smaller loads. “Some services are suspended further upstream on the Kaub gauge, where low water has severely restricted navigation, while large volumes are being shifted to rail and truck, but alternative capacity is limited,” said Mr Ginckels. “Cargo is still moving, but carrying capacity is sharply reduced, transport costs have risen, transit times are longer and less predictable, while inland terminals, rail networks, and trucking markets are absorbing displaced cargo at higher cost and delays.” Some 35% of box movements along the Dutch hinterland tend to travel by inland waterway, meaning that even seeing a part of that traffic transferred to alternative modes piles massive pressure onto already constrained transport networks. Back in August, Metro Global stated that more than 200 trucks would be required to replace lost barge capacity, and while low water levels have become part and parcel of the Rhine’s summer months in recent years, the persisting into October presented additional problems.
